title: The Hidden Curriculum for Adults: Why School Norms Shape Teachers More Than Policies
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Leaders trying to change organizational culture through persuasion alone are fighting the wrong battle, Hughes argues: most professional behavior is governed by unconscious social norms rather than conscious deliberation over policy or evidence. Drawing on Kahneman's System 1 thinking and McCrea's model of motivation as an unconscious investment engine, she shows that people constantly scan their environment for cues about what leaders and colleagues actually reward, and adjust their behavior accordingly before ever consciously weighing a rationale or a slide deck. Social Identity Theory (Tajfel and Turner) explains why this matters for anyone leading a team: people ask 'what do people like me do around here?' far more often than 'what do I believe is best?', making the informal culture a leader inherits or builds the single biggest lever on team behavior. Hughes contrasts two organizational cultures — one where cynicism, presenteeism, and martyrdom are quietly rewarded, and one where curiosity and sustainable effort are the norm — and stresses that neither emerges from a written policy; both are learned by new members within days. For leaders specifically, the practical implication is that culture change requires engineering the environment rather than persuading through argument: modelling the desired behavior, making it visible when respected people practice it, and building psychological safety so team members feel able to admit uncertainty and ask for help. Citing Edmondson's research on psychological safety and Barsade's work on emotional contagion, Hughes argues that team wellbeing and performance are collective, norm-driven outcomes rather than individual traits — meaning a leader's own visible habits function as the most powerful lever available for shaping how an entire team behaves. The piece closes with a direct challenge to leadership: norms exist in every organization whether or not anyone designs them, so the only real choice a leader has is whether to shape them deliberately or let them be set by the loudest voices in the room.
points: Most team behavior is governed by unconscious social norms rather than conscious persuasion — leaders who rely on rationale, evidence, and beautifully formatted plans to change culture are appealing to a slow deliberate system that rarely drives day-to-day behavior.

Social Identity Theory shows people constantly ask 'what do people like me do around here?' rather than weighing their own independent judgment — making a leader's visible modelling of behavior a far more powerful culture lever than any written policy.

Leaders who want collaboration, honesty about mistakes, or sustainable working hours should make those behaviors visible in respected people, rather than simply asking for them — visibility of the norm is what spreads it through a team.

Psychological safety (Edmondson) and emotional contagion (Barsade) mean that a leader's own tolerance for uncertainty and mistakes sets the emotional tone for the whole team; cynicism spreads as readily as optimism and trust.

Team wellbeing is a collective, norm-driven achievement rather than an individual characteristic — a leader cannot delegate culture change to a wellbeing initiative while the underlying norms (who gets praised, who is quietly mocked for leaving on time) continue to teach the opposite lesson.
quotes: Schools spend enormous amounts of time writing policies that describe how people should behave. Yet, as Doug Lemov argues, norms almost always prove more influential than rules because they shape behaviour beneath conscious awareness. They are “largely invisible and unconscious,” yet often override formal policies because they determine what people come to regard as normal.

Social Identity Theory helps explain why these environments diverge so dramatically. Tajfel and Turner (1979) argued that our sense of self is deeply connected to the groups to which we belong. We constantly seek cues about the behaviours that signal membership. The question is rarely, What do I personally believe is best? It is far more often, What do people like me do around here?

Perhaps this also explains why leaders so often struggle to change culture through persuasion alone. We explain the rationale. We share the evidence. We produce beautifully formatted implementation plans. Yet if heuristics guide much of human behaviour automatically, leadership becomes less about convincing people and more about shaping environments in which desirable behaviours become the obvious behaviours.

When experienced teachers openly admit uncertainty, psychological safety begins to grow. Edmondson’s (1999) research demonstrates that teams learn more effectively when individuals feel safe enough to acknowledge mistakes, ask questions and seek feedback without fear of embarrassment. Likewise, Barsade’s (2002) work on emotional contagion reminds us that emotions spread rapidly through organisations. Cynicism is contagious, but luckily, so are optimism, generosity and trust.

Every school is constantly teaching its staff what professionalism looks like, whether intentionally or accidentally. The question is not whether norms exist - they always do. The question is whether we are shaping them deliberately or merely inheriting them from the loudest voices in the room. Because long after the policies have been rewritten, the PowerPoint slides archived and the implementation plans forgotten, the norms remain.
